body:
Classifying a Satellite by Its Function

Satellites can be classified by what they are designed to do. A communication satellite relays signals. An Earth-observation satellite measures radiation associated with land, water or the atmosphere. A navigation satellite transmits signals that help receivers determine position and time. A scientific satellite observes physical phenomena for research.

These categories describe the main purpose of a satellite. Some satellites carry several instruments and provide more than one service. For example, meteorological satellites may also support data relay and search-and-rescue systems.

System or satelliteMain roleIllustrative application
INSAT and GSAT familiesCommunication and, in selected satellites, meteorologyTelevision, telecommunication and weather services
EDUSAT or GSAT-3Dedicated educational communicationSatellite-based educational broadcasting
INSAT-3DSMeteorological observationsCloud monitoring, atmospheric observations and cyclone support
IRS and ResourcesatNatural-resource observationCrop, land and resource mapping
CartosatHigh-resolution Earth imagingCartography and urban planning
RISAT and radar-based EOS missionsRadar observationImaging during cloud cover and flood assessment
Oceansat and EOS-06Ocean observationsOcean colour, surface winds and marine studies
NavICPositioning, navigation and timingLand and marine navigation

Communication and Meteorological Satellites

India's INSAT system developed as a multipurpose satellite programme serving communication and meteorological needs. The related GSAT family includes communication satellites with different capacities and purposes.

A communication satellite receives signals from an Earth station and retransmits them to another location. This allows television broadcasting, telecommunication and connectivity over large areas. Its function is different from that of a remote-sensing satellite, which observes physical features and conditions.

EDUSAT, also known as GSAT-3, was launched in 2004 for educational services. It is an important historical example of applying space technology to education; the launch date should not be confused with the satellite's present operational status.

INSAT-3DS was launched by GSLV-F14 on 17 February 2024. Its meteorological instruments support cloud imaging and measurements of atmospheric conditions. Such information assists the India Meteorological Department (IMD) in weather analysis and forecasting.

Earth-Observation Satellite Families

Indian Remote Sensing (IRS) satellites and later Earth-observation missions help monitor natural resources. Different instruments are suited to different purposes.

  • Resourcesat: crop acreage, agricultural conditions and land-resource monitoring.
  • Cartosat: detailed mapping of terrain, infrastructure and settlements.
  • RISAT: radar-based observations useful when optical images are obstructed by cloud.
  • Oceansat: ocean colour, surface winds and marine environmental observations.

The term EOS means Earth Observation Satellite. The EOS naming system does not mean that every satellite has the same sensor. For example, EOS-04 is a radar-imaging mission, whereas EOS-06 belongs to the Oceansat series.

NavIC: India's Regional Navigation System

NavIC stands for Navigation with Indian Constellation. It developed from the Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System (IRNSS). It is India's independent regional satellite navigation system, designed to serve India and an area extending approximately 1,500 km beyond its boundaries.

The original NavIC constellation was designed around 7 satellites: 3 geostationary and 4 inclined geosynchronous satellites. These figures describe the original constellation design; they must not be used as an unverified count of fully operational satellites at a later date.

NavIC provides a Standard Positioning Service (SPS) for civilian users and a Restricted Service (RS) for authorised users. It can support navigation on roads and at sea, vehicle tracking, surveying and precise timing. Newer NVS-series satellites introduce civilian L1 signals alongside existing navigation signal bands.

GPS is the United States' global navigation satellite system. NavIC is an Indian regional system. GAGAN, or GPS Aided Geo Augmented Navigation, is a satellite-based augmentation system developed through cooperation between ISRO and the Airports Authority of India (AAI) for civil aviation. GAGAN improves navigation support; it is not the same system as NavIC.

Navigation Satellite Status at the Content Cutoff

Status as of 4 November 2026: ISRO lists NVS-01, launched on 29 May 2023, as operational for positioning, navigation and timing services. NVS-02, launched by GSLV-F15 on 29 January 2025, is listed as not operational.

NVS-03 was launched by GSLV-F18 on 30 October 2026. ISRO's update dated 31 October 2026 reported a successful first orbit-raising manoeuvre and stated that further manoeuvres were planned to reach the intended geosynchronous orbit. That update confirmed launch and initial orbital progress, not completed entry into operational navigation service. A satellite's launch status must not be treated as proof that its service is operational.

Prelims focus

  • INSAT and GSAT: communication; IRS and Resourcesat: resource observation.
  • INSAT-3DS: meteorological satellite launched on 17 February 2024.
  • Cartosat: detailed cartographic imaging; RISAT: radar-based imaging.
  • NavIC: Indian regional navigation system; original design involved 7 satellites.
  • GAGAN: aviation-navigation augmentation through ISRO and AAI.
  • Trap: A successfully launched navigation satellite is not necessarily operational.

[NCERT, The Earth: Our Habitat, Class 6, chapter 1, p. 5; ISRO, Spacecraft Missions, Earth Observation, Communication and Navigation Satellite entries, status consulted 4 November 2026; ISRO, Satellite Navigation Services, NavIC and GAGAN sections; ISRO, GSLV-F18/NVS-03 Mission, 30 October 2026; ISRO, Orbit manoeuvring of NVS-03 spacecraft, 31 October 2026; ISRO, Launch Missions, INSAT-3DS and EOS-06 entries.]

body:
Exploration Missions Have Different Objectives

Not every space mission is designed to observe the Earth. Some spacecraft study the Moon, Mars, the Sun or distant astronomical objects. Others demonstrate a technology that may be useful for future missions.

The mission type must be identified precisely. An orbiter studies a body while revolving around it. A lander reaches its surface. A rover moves across the surface to make observations. A technology-demonstration mission tests a capability rather than primarily providing an everyday public service.

The Chandrayaan Missions

Chandrayaan-1: Lunar Orbital Exploration

Chandrayaan-1, launched by PSLV-C11 on 22 October 2008, was India's first lunar mission. Its scientific instruments studied the Moon's surface and composition. Observations from the mission contributed important evidence for water and hydroxyl molecules on the lunar surface.

The mission also carried a Moon Impact Probe. Its impact with the surface was not a controlled soft landing. Thus, Chandrayaan-1 should principally be understood as an orbital scientific mission rather than a successful rover mission.

Chandrayaan-2: Orbiter Success and Lander Attempt

Chandrayaan-2 was launched on 22 July 2019 by GSLV Mk-III. It carried an orbiter, the Vikram lander and the Pragyan rover. The spacecraft entered lunar orbit successfully.

During Vikram's landing attempt on 7 September 2019, communication was lost. The planned soft landing was not achieved. However, the orbiter continued its scientific work, including observations of the lunar surface and minerals. It is therefore inaccurate to describe every component of Chandrayaan-2 as unsuccessful.

Chandrayaan-3: Successful Soft Landing

Chandrayaan-3 was launched on 14 July 2023 by LVM3-M4. On 23 August 2023, its Vikram lander successfully made a soft landing in the southern high-latitude or south-polar region of the Moon. The Pragyan rover was deployed and carried out surface investigations.

The lander and rover provided information about conditions at and near the surface, including temperature, elemental composition and the local environment. The mission demonstrated controlled lunar landing and rover operations. It was not a lunar sample-return mission, and its landing site was near the lunar south pole, not at the exact pole.

Mars Orbiter Mission

India's Mars Orbiter Mission (MOM), also known as Mangalyaan, was launched by PSLV-C25 on 5 November 2013 and entered orbit around Mars on 24 September 2014.

It studied the Martian surface and atmosphere using scientific instruments. Its planned mission life was much shorter than its actual period of operation. ISRO reported the conclusion of the mission in 2022. MOM was a Mars orbiter, not a Mars lander.

Studying the Sun and the Universe

AstroSat, launched on 28 September 2015, was India's first dedicated multiwavelength space-astronomy observatory. It observes astronomical objects using instruments operating at different wavelengths, including ultraviolet and X-rays.

Aditya-L1, launched by PSLV-C57 on 2 September 2023, studies the Sun, including its outer atmosphere, solar wind and solar activity. It entered a halo orbit around the Sun-Earth L1 point on 6 January 2024. The observation location is approximately 1.5 million km from Earth towards the Sun.

The L1 point is a location in the Sun-Earth gravitational system that provides a useful position for sustained solar observations. Aditya-L1 did not land on the Sun. It follows a controlled orbit around the L1 region.

XPoSat, launched on 1 January 2024, is an X-ray astronomy mission designed to study the polarisation and other properties of X-rays from astronomical sources. Its purpose differs from Aditya-L1's solar observations and from AstroSat's broader multiwavelength astronomy.

Technology Demonstration and Human Spaceflight

SpaDeX, the Space Docking Experiment, was launched on 30 December 2024 by PSLV-C60. Two spacecraft successfully docked on 16 January 2025; undocking was demonstrated on 13 March 2025. Docking means bringing separate spacecraft together and connecting them in orbit. This technology can support future spacecraft assembly and human-spaceflight activities.

Gaganyaan is India's human-spaceflight programme. It includes the development and testing of crew-related systems and a human-rated launch vehicle. Gaganyaan should not be confused with SpaDeX, which used uncrewed spacecraft, or with an Indian astronaut's participation in a separate international mission.

Prelims focus

  • Chandrayaan-1: launched in 2008; important evidence for lunar water-related molecules.
  • Chandrayaan-2: launched in 2019; orbiter successful, lander attempt unsuccessful.
  • Chandrayaan-3: launched on 14 July 2023; soft landing on 23 August 2023.
  • Mangalyaan: launched in 2013; entered Mars orbit in 2014.
  • Aditya-L1: halo-orbit insertion on 6 January 2024; solar observations near Sun-Earth L1.
  • Trap: An orbiter, a lander, a rover and a docking experiment demonstrate different capabilities.
